Run a sample of the carrier's manifests, refine the extraction prompt on the results, then batch all 200.
Submit them with the rest under a tightened extract_manifest schema, so a misread layout is rejected on arrival.
Extract this carrier's manifests synchronously for the first week, then fold them into the nightly batch run.
cards.a: B. Run a sample of the carrier's manifests, refine the extraction prompt on the results, then batch all 200.
cards.explanation:
A. Resubmitting failed custom_ids is the documented way to handle batch failures and is worth planning for anyway. A layout the prompt has never met fails as a class rather than at random, so most of the 200 come back for a second paid run.

B. Correct. Refining the prompt on a sample before batch-processing a large volume is what raises the first-pass success rate, and a dozen sample manifests cost a fraction of the resubmission a bad first night would force.

C. A tighter schema does keep malformed extractions out of the AP ledger and is good hygiene on any new document type. Rejection is not extraction: the batch is paid for in full and every rejected manifest still has to be worked afterwards.

D. Synchronous calls surface each failure immediately and would certainly expose the new layout fast. It forgoes the batch saving for a week on volume that has no latency requirement, to learn what a sample of a dozen answers in an hour.

Key principle: A batch is committed and paid for all at once, so first-pass quality has to be established before submission. Prompt refinement on a sample is what buys that, and it is cheapest on a document type nothing has been tuned against.

cards.q: Shipping manifests sometimes record quantities informally, such as "2 pallets (48 cases)". The extraction records 2 on some manifests and 48 on others with no discernible pattern. You are adding three few-shot examples of informal quantity phrasing. What makes them most likely to generalise to phrasings you have not seen yet?
options: Each example covers one more of the specific phrasings seen in the last month of incoming manifests.
The examples sit at the very end of the prompt, immediately before the document being processed.
Each example shows the complete schema output, so every field is demonstrated alongside quantity.
Each example states why the chosen unit was picked over the plausible alternative in that document.
cards.a: D. Each example states why the chosen unit was picked over the plausible alternative in that document.
cards.explanation:
A. Covering observed phrasings guarantees those exact cases are handled, and for a fixed vocabulary that would be enough. Manifest phrasing is open-ended, so pure pattern coverage produces a lookup table: the model matches the demonstrated strings and is back to guessing on the fourth phrasing that shows up next month.

B. Placement near the document is a sound prompt-construction habit and keeps the examples salient. It changes where the model reads the examples, not what they teach - three examples that only show inputs and outputs teach the same thing wherever they sit in the prompt.

C. Showing the full schema output does reinforce the overall shape of a correct extraction, which is useful when several fields are unstable. Here only quantity is unstable, and padding each example with the other fields dilutes the signal about unit choice rather than sharpening it.

D. Correct. Examples that show the reasoning - why cases rather than pallets was the right unit here - teach the judgment rather than the string. That is what lets the model generalise to novel phrasings instead of matching pre-specified cases.

Key principle: Few-shot examples for ambiguous cases should show why one reading was chosen over a plausible alternative. Reasoning generalises to novel inputs; input-output pairs alone only cover what they demonstrate.

cards.q: Incoming files arrive unlabelled and may be a supplier invoice, a purchase order, or a shipping manifest. You have defined extract_invoice, extract_po, and extract_manifest, each with its own JSON schema, and every file must come back as schema-valid structured data. Which configuration fits?
options: Set tool_choice to "auto" and let the model return text describing the file when it is unsure.
Force extract_invoice by name for every file, then correct the mismatched ones downstream.
Classify the document type in a prior call, then run the single extraction tool that result names.
Set tool_choice to "any", so the model must call one of the three tools but chooses which one.
cards.a: D. Set tool_choice to "any", so the model must call one of the three tools but chooses which one.
cards.explanation:
A. "auto" preserves the model's option to explain rather than extract, which is genuinely useful when a file might be unreadable. It also means an unsure model returns free text with no schema at all, which is the one outcome this pipeline cannot accept.

B. Forcing a named tool does guarantee structured output, and forced selection is the right mode when one specific extraction must run. Forcing the invoice schema onto purchase orders and manifests produces valid JSON in the wrong shape, which is worse than a parse failure because it passes validation.

C. A classify-then-extract split is a real architecture and gives you an auditable document-type decision. It costs a second call on every file and adds a failure mode of its own, when "any" already delivers the guarantee in one call by letting the model select the schema.

D. Correct. "any" guarantees a tool call - so the response is always schema-compliant structured data - while leaving the choice of which schema to the model. That is precisely the case where several extraction schemas exist and the document type is not known in advance.

Key principle: tool_choice "any" guarantees a tool call while leaving schema selection to the model - the right setting when multiple extraction schemas exist and the document type is unknown. Forced selection is for when one specific tool must run.

cards.q: About 15% of purchase orders state no delivery date anywhere on the page, yet delivery_date comes back populated on nearly all of them - sometimes copying the order date, sometimes a plausible invention. The field is currently marked required in the extract_po schema. What is the right correction?
options: Keep delivery_date required and define a sentinel value of "NOT_STATED" for the purchase orders that carry no date.
Add a validation rule rejecting any delivery_date equal to the order date, then retry those extractions.
Make delivery_date optional and nullable, so the model can return no value rather than satisfy a requirement.
Add a delivery_date_confidence score to the schema and route the low-confidence purchase orders to review.
cards.a: C. Make delivery_date optional and nullable, so the model can return no value rather than satisfy a requirement.
cards.explanation:
A. A sentinel does give absence somewhere to go, and reserved values are a long-standing convention in flat file formats. The field stays required and stops being a date: every downstream consumer has to special-case the string, and a model that misses the convention supplies a plausible date instead.

B. Rejecting dates equal to the order date catches one recognisable fabrication pattern and is cheap to implement. It only catches that pattern - the plausible inventions that are not the order date pass straight through - and the retry re-runs against the same required field, so the model fabricates again.

C. Correct. The model is fabricating because the schema requires a value and the document has none. Making the field optional and nullable removes the pressure, so absent information is reported as absent instead of invented.

D. Field-level confidence plus routing is a sound way to direct scarce reviewer attention, and it would surface some of these. It leaves the root cause running - the schema still demands a value - so reviewers spend their capacity deleting fabrications the pipeline should never have produced.

Key principle: Required schema fields on information that may genuinely be absent push the model to fabricate. Design fields the source may not contain as optional and nullable so absence can be represented.

cards.q: The validation-retry loop resends the document, the failed extraction, and the specific validation error, and clears most failures on the first retry. One cluster does not: manifests fail three retries every night on carrier_tracking_number, a value the carrier only ever issues in a separate file the pipeline does not pass in. What should change?
options: Raise the retry ceiling for that field and include each failed attempt in the follow-up request.
Stop retrying it, return null, and source the tracking number from the carrier file downstream.
Add few-shot examples of manifests where the tracking number sits in an unusual page position.
Escalate the failing manifests to human reviewers, who can look each tracking number up by hand.
cards.a: B. Stop retrying it, return null, and source the tracking number from the carrier file downstream.
cards.explanation:
A. More retries with richer error history is the correct instinct for format and structure failures, and it is why the loop works on everything else. Here the information is not in the document at all, so every additional attempt costs tokens and latency to rediscover the same absence - or invents a value to end the loop.

B. Correct. Retry helps when the model mis-formatted or mis-structured available information. It cannot help when the required value is absent from the source, so the extraction should record null and the join to the carrier file should happen where that data actually lives.

C. Positional few-shot examples are the right fix when a value is present but in an unexpected place, which is a real failure mode for varied manifests. The stem rules that out - the number is issued in a separate file - so the examples would demonstrate an extraction that cannot occur.

D. Human escalation guarantees the ledger eventually gets a tracking number, and escalation is appropriate for ambiguous or contradictory sources. This case is neither ambiguous nor a judgment call: a reviewer would simply open the carrier file, which a downstream join can do automatically and at no marginal cost.

Key principle: Retry-with-error-feedback fixes format and structure errors. When the required information is absent from the source document, no number of retries will produce it - return null and obtain the value where it exists.

cards.q: Since extraction moved to tool use with strict JSON schemas, parse failures have gone to zero. The AP ledger still receives invoices whose line_items do not add up to the stated_total printed on the page. Which change surfaces these before the ledger accepts them?
options: Tighten the numeric types on each of the line item fields so the schema rejects malformed amounts on arrival.
Add a prompt instruction telling the model to check its arithmetic before it returns the extraction.
Compare each invoice total against the matching purchase order and flag the pairs that disagree.
Extract calculated_total from the line items alongside stated_total and flag invoices where they differ.
cards.a: D. Extract calculated_total from the line items alongside stated_total and flag invoices where they differ.
cards.explanation:
A. Stricter numeric typing is good schema hygiene and blocks a class of malformed values. It operates on individual fields in isolation, though, and every value in these invoices is already well-formed - the defect is the relationship between the line items and the total, which no per-field type can express.

B. Asking for a self-check costs nothing and will catch some arithmetic slips, so it is a reasonable addition. It is also probabilistic on exactly the kind of error the model just made, and it produces no artefact the pipeline can gate on - the ledger has nothing to test.

C. A three-way match against the purchase order is a genuinely valuable AP control and catches billing disputes. It answers a different question - whether the invoice matches what was ordered - and misses the internal inconsistency here, where an invoice can disagree with itself while matching its PO.

D. Correct. Having the model produce the sum it derives from the line items as well as the total printed on the page turns a semantic error into a machine-checkable discrepancy the pipeline can flag deterministically.

Key principle: Strict schemas via tool use eliminate syntax errors but not semantic ones. Extracting a derived value alongside the stated one converts a semantic inconsistency into an explicit, testable discrepancy.

cards.q: The AP ledger accepts four payment-terms codes and nothing else, but payment_terms comes back from extract_invoice as whatever the invoice printed - "Net 30", "30 days net", "payable within one month". The loader's phrase-to-code mapping table gains an entry most weeks. What is the right correction?
options: Grow the loader's mapping table into a normalisation service the AP team can extend themselves whenever a new phrasing turns up.
Instruct the extraction prompt to return one of the four ledger codes, listing each code beside a sample phrase an invoice might print.
Declare payment_terms in the tool's JSON schema as an enum of the four ledger codes the AP ledger is willing to accept.
Validate each extraction against the four codes and send any invoice carrying an unrecognised phrase back through the retry loop.
cards.a: C. Declare payment_terms in the tool's JSON schema as an enum of the four ledger codes the AP ledger is willing to accept.
cards.explanation:
A. Owning the mapping gives the AP team a change they can make without a pipeline release, and it does keep the ledger clean. It leaves the model free to phrase the field however the document does on all 1,400 nightly extractions, so the table is permanently chasing wording that has already shipped.

B. Naming the four codes in the prompt with a sample phrase for each raises conformance sharply and is worth doing alongside any schema work. On its own it constrains nothing - a fifth value is still a legal response, and at nightly volume the occasional stray reaches the ledger.

C. Correct. An enum in the tool's JSON schema makes those four codes the only values the extraction is able to return, so the ledger's constraint is enforced where the output is produced rather than translated after the fact.

D. Rejecting unrecognised values does guarantee the ledger only ever sees the four codes, and the retry loop already exists to handle validation failures. It spends a second extraction call correcting a shape the schema could have made unrepresentable in the first place.

Key principle: When a downstream system accepts a closed set of values, put that set in the tool's JSON schema. Prompt wording and downstream mapping both act after the model has already chosen; the schema decides what can be produced at all.

cards.q: Your team is moving the nightly reconciliation of 1,400 documents onto the Message Batches API and is writing the code that consumes the results. Which two statements about that API should shape the design?
options: Batch pricing halves the cost only for the requests that finish inside the first hour of the window.
A batch may take up to 24 hours to complete, and it carries no guaranteed latency SLA.
A batch request will pause for a client-side tool result and resume once the caller returns it.
A single failed document forces the whole batch to be resubmitted, since custom_id is per batch.
Responses can come back in a different order from submission, so pair them by custom_id.
cards.a: B. A batch may take up to 24 hours to complete, and it carries no guaranteed latency SLA.; E. Responses can come back in a different order from submission, so pair them by custom_id.
cards.explanation:
A. The 50% saving is real, which makes this tempting, but it is not conditional on completion time. Attaching the discount to a first-hour deadline would invent a latency expectation the API explicitly does not offer, and would push the team to build monitoring against a threshold that does not exist.

B. Correct. The window can run up to 24 hours with no latency guarantee, so the consuming code must be built as an asynchronous poll-and-collect rather than assuming results are ready by a given clock time.

C. Tool calling itself does work in batch requests, so this is close enough to true to be dangerous. Multi-turn tool calling is not supported within a single batch request - tools cannot execute mid-request and return results - so any enrichment lookup must be a separate stage in the pipeline.

D. Handling failures by resubmission is right, and resubmitting only what failed is the documented approach. custom_id is what identifies the individual failed documents, which is precisely what lets you resubmit that subset - often with a modification such as chunking an oversized document - rather than the entire batch.

E. Correct. Results are not guaranteed to arrive in submission order, so the consuming code must correlate each response to its request by custom_id. Pairing by position will silently attach extractions to the wrong documents.

Key principle: The Batches API trades latency guarantees for cost: results arrive within an up-to-24-hour window, in any order, correlated only by custom_id. Design the consumer around identity, never position.

cards.q: To catch values placed in the wrong schema field, the pipeline appends "now re-check your extraction for mistakes" to the same request that produced it. The self-check almost never overturns a value, yet AP reviewers keep finding wrong-field placements in the output. Which change catches more of them?
options: Send the document and the extraction to a second instance that has no view of the first one's reasoning.
Enable extended thinking on the extraction call so the model reasons longer before committing to values.
Have the same request produce the extraction twice under different field orderings and reconcile the pair.
Add a per-field confidence score to the schema and route the lowest-scoring fields to an AP reviewer.
cards.a: A. Send the document and the extraction to a second instance that has no view of the first one's reasoning.
cards.explanation:
A. Correct. A model that just produced an extraction still holds the reasoning that produced it and is unlikely to question its own decision. An independent instance seeing only the document and the result evaluates it fresh, which is what surfaces the subtle placements.

B. Extended thinking does improve the quality of the initial extraction and is worth having on a hard task. It deepens the same reasoning chain rather than challenging it, so the model arrives at its answer more thoroughly and remains just as committed to it during the self-check.

C. Two passes do expose fields the model is unstable on, and a disagreement between them is a usable signal worth logging. Both passes run inside the request already committed to a reading, so a confident wrong placement is reproduced rather than challenged.

D. Field-level scores are a sound way to aim scarce reviewer attention and cost one property in the schema. The score comes from the session that made the placement, and a value put confidently in the wrong field scores high, so these misplacements stay out of the queue.

Key principle: A model retains its generation reasoning and is poor at questioning its own output in the same session. Independent review instances without that prior context catch subtle errors that self-review instructions miss.

cards.q: Invoices arrive throughout the day, and the AP ledger's service agreement requires each one posted within 30 hours of receipt. Extraction runs on the Message Batches API, whose processing window can reach 24 hours. The pipeline submits one batch at 02:00 covering everything received since the previous run. What submission schedule meets the agreement?
options: Keep the nightly batch and flag the requests as high priority, so the queue returns the overnight submission sooner
Submit a batch every four hours, so the longest wait for a submission plus the processing window stays under 30 hours
Split the nightly run into six batches submitted together at 02:00, so each carries fewer documents and finishes sooner
Extract invoices received after 22:00 synchronously, so the arrivals closest to the cutoff are not held for the batch
cards.a: B. Submit a batch every four hours, so the longest wait for a submission plus the processing window stays under 30 hours
cards.explanation:
A. Priority ordering would help if the API exposed one to raise; the batch window carries no guaranteed latency SLA. An invoice arriving at 02:05 still waits almost 24 hours before it is even submitted.

B. Correct. A document waits at most four hours for the next submission and the batch itself may take 24, so the ceiling is 28 hours, inside the agreement with margin left for the posting step.

C. Smaller batches carry less work each, and nothing in the API promises a faster completion for a smaller batch. Submitting all six at 02:00 leaves the arrival-to-submission wait exactly where it was.

D. Synchronous calls return in seconds and are the right choice for genuinely blocking work. Applied to late arrivals alone it pays full price for part of the volume while the 02:05 arrivals still wait a full day.

Key principle: Batch cadence is arithmetic: worst-case wait for the next submission plus the 24-hour window has to fit inside the SLA. Resizing or reordering batches does not change that wait; submitting more often does.

cards.q: For a three-issue dispute the coordinator concatenates the identity check, the order history and the billing findings into one long prompt, with billing in the middle. Identity and order details reach the customer reply; the billing findings are routinely missing from it. Which two changes address this positional effect?
options: Place a key-findings summary at the beginning of the aggregated prompt
Re-order the three blocks by recency so the newest findings sit first
Drop the billing block and re-fetch those findings on demand instead
Organise the detail beneath an explicit section header for each block
Raise the reply's max token limit so all three issues fit in one message
cards.a: A. Place a key-findings summary at the beginning of the aggregated prompt; D. Organise the detail beneath an explicit section header for each block
cards.explanation:
A. Correct. Long inputs are processed reliably at the beginning and the end, so a summary of all three blocks placed first puts the billing findings where they will be read.

B. Keeps the freshest work near the front and is a sensible ordering rule in a long session, but it only moves which block occupies the middle; whichever one lands there is omitted next.

C. Cuts the prompt down and would help if the failure were volumetric. It is positional, so re-fetching returns the same findings to the same weak position, at the cost of an extra call.

D. Correct. Explicit section headers organising the detailed results are the guide's second mitigation for position effects, giving the middle material structure the model can locate.

E. Prevents a long resolution message being cut off mid-sentence, a real failure elsewhere. Here the reply completes; it simply never contains the billing material in the first place.

Key principle: Findings in the middle of a long input can be omitted while the beginning and end come through. The remedy is placement and structure, summary first, explicit section headers, not trimming.

cards.q: get_customer returns three accounts matching "J. Alvarez" in the same city. The agent currently selects the one with the most recent order and continues into the refund flow. What should it do instead?
options: Escalate to a human at once, since ambiguous identity is a policy gap the agent cannot resolve alone
Read back the most recent order's details and let the customer correct the record if it looks wrong
Rank the candidate accounts by profile completeness and proceed with the highest-scoring match found
Ask the customer for one more identifier, such as an order number or the email on the account
cards.a: D. Ask the customer for one more identifier, such as an order number or the email on the account
cards.explanation:
A. Is the right instinct when policy is silent on a request, and it does prevent a wrong-account refund, but handing off a question the customer can answer in one turn spends human capacity needlessly.

B. Involves the customer rather than guessing silently, which is better than the current behavior, but it anchors on a guess and invites a distracted customer to confirm someone else's order.

C. Replaces one heuristic with a more defensible one, and completeness scoring is useful for ranking search results, but any heuristic still resolves identity without evidence from the customer.

D. Correct. Multiple matches call for clarification, not selection. One additional identifier resolves the ambiguity from authoritative input and keeps the case in first-contact resolution.

Key principle: When tool results return multiple matches, request an additional identifier rather than selecting heuristically. Escalation is for explicit customer requests, policy gaps, and genuine lack of progress, not for questions the customer can answer.

cards.q: The billing subagent's invoice query times out after two internal retries. It returns "billing data unavailable" to the coordinator, which then abandons the entire resolution, including the damaged-item claim it had already substantiated. What should the subagent return?
options: An empty result marked successful, so the coordinator proceeds with the concerns it can still resolve
The same status plus a directive telling the coordinator to escalate this ticket to a human reviewer
The failure type, the query it attempted, any partial results, and the alternatives still available
A retry request asking the coordinator to re-delegate the identical query after a short backoff period
cards.a: C. The failure type, the query it attempted, any partial results, and the alternatives still available
cards.explanation:
A. Keeps the workflow alive, which is the improvement being sought, but it disguises a failure as a valid empty result, so the coordinator reports "no billing issues found" for an issue it never saw.

B. Ensures a human eventually sees the case and is appropriate once options are exhausted, but it escalates the whole ticket over one unavailable subquery instead of resolving what is already resolvable.

C. Correct. Structured error context lets the coordinator decide intelligently: keep the substantiated claim, annotate the billing gap, and choose whether an alternative path is worth attempting.

D. Delegates recovery upward, and backoff is the right response to a transient failure, but the subagent already retried twice, and the coordinator has no information to decide differently.

Key principle: Generic failure statuses hide the context a coordinator needs, and both silent suppression and whole-workflow termination are anti-patterns. Propagate failure type, what was attempted, partial results, and alternatives.

cards.q: Three days into the HTTP client migration, the session has filled with verbose discovery output and answers about atlas's wrapper classes have started drifting toward typical adapter patterns. Select the TWO moves that address this.
options: Run /memory to release the context that the discovery output has been consuming.
Run /compact to reduce context usage now that the window is full of discovery output.
Re-enter the work with --resume so the session reloads with a smaller footprint.
Keep a scratchpad file of key findings and consult it when answering later questions.
Set context: fork on the session so the verbose discovery output lands elsewhere.
cards.a: B. Run /compact to reduce context usage now that the window is full of discovery output.; D. Keep a scratchpad file of key findings and consult it when answering later questions.
cards.explanation:
A. /memory is a real command, and its name makes it sound like a context-pressure tool. What it actually does is report which memory files are loaded, for diagnosing inconsistent behaviour across sessions.

B. Correct. /compact is named for exactly this state: reducing context usage during an extended exploration session once the window has filled with verbose discovery output.

C. --resume does continue a named investigation across working sessions, which is useful here on other days. Resumption restores prior context rather than shrinking it, so it does not relieve a full window.

D. Correct. A scratchpad file of key findings, referenced when answering later questions, is the named counter to context degradation, because the findings live outside the window.

E. context: fork is real, but it is SKILL.md frontmatter that runs a skill in an isolated sub-agent context. It is set on a skill, not on a running session, so it cannot be applied to this one mid-migration.

Key principle: Two named mechanisms cover this state: /compact for reducing context usage when an extended session fills with verbose discovery output, and scratchpad files that record key findings outside the window. /memory, --resume and context: fork are each named for a different job.

cards.q: Three days into the HTTP client migration, the session working packages/ingest has spent forty minutes on one transitive dependency conflict: three variations of the same fix, the same four files re-read, nothing new learned. The team's rule hands work back to a maintainer when the agent's self-reported confidence falls below a threshold, and it has not fired. What should trigger the handoff?
options: Repeated attempts that surface no new information, the signal that the run cannot make further progress
A wall-clock cap on the session, returning any package that takes longer than thirty minutes to a maintainer
The agent's own commentary turning negative, escalating once its summaries start calling the work blocked
A raised iteration budget and one more attempt, since dependency conflicts here have cleared on a retry
cards.a: A. Repeated attempts that surface no new information, the signal that the run cannot make further progress
cards.explanation:
A. Correct. Inability to make meaningful progress is the escalation trigger, and it is observable: attempts that revisit the same files and produce the same failure are evidence the run has stopped moving, whatever it reports about itself.

B. A timeout bounds the damage and is worth keeping as a backstop. It fires on slow work as readily as on stuck work, so it hands back sessions that are progressing and keeps ones that stalled in the first five minutes.

C. Tone is easy to read off a transcript and does correlate loosely with trouble. Sentiment is not a measure of whether progress is possible, and a run can narrate confidently while looping on one unresolved conflict.

D. Retrying is the right response to a transient failure and costs one iteration. Three attempts have already returned the same result, which is evidence the blocker is not transient and not inside what this run can resolve.

Key principle: Escalate on an observable lack of progress, not on elapsed time or the model's own confidence: neither is a reliable proxy for whether the work can still move.

cards.q: The doc-analysis subagent returns each finding as its full reasoning chain plus the entire source excerpt, roughly 4,000 tokens apiece. With 30 findings passed in, the synthesis subagent's input is nearly full before it starts, and its drafts now omit whole middle sections. What is the most effective change?
options: Have the coordinator summarize all 30 findings into a short brief before it spawns the synthesis subagent.
Pass the findings in relevance order, strongest first, so the most important material sits in early context.
Have doc-analysis return key facts, citations, and relevance scores instead of full excerpts and chains.
Split synthesis across three subagents of ten findings each, then merge their three drafts in a later pass.
cards.a: C. Have doc-analysis return key facts, citations, and relevance scores instead of full excerpts and chains.
cards.explanation:
A. A coordinator-side summary does shrink the input and keeps synthesis focused, but compressing findings after the fact is where numbers, dates, and source attributions get flattened into vague prose.

B. Ordering by relevance does put the strongest findings where a long input is read most reliably, and it costs nothing to try. It rearranges an input that is still far too large, so whatever lands in the middle is dropped just the same.

C. Correct. When a downstream agent has a limited context budget, the fix is upstream: have the producing agent emit structured findings, facts, citations, relevance scores, rather than verbose content and reasoning.

D. Sharding avoids the overflow and is a reasonable pattern for very large corpora, at the cost of a merge pass and of each shard synthesizing without sight of the others' findings.

Key principle: Trim at the source. Verbose tool and subagent output consumes context disproportionately to its relevance, and reshaping what upstream agents return beats reorganizing or compressing it downstream.

cards.q: Two credible sources put the market at $4.2B and $6.8B, and doc-analysis escalates the pair to the coordinator as a contradiction. One figure is a full-year 2023 total; the other covers a single quarter of 2025. Neither finding records the period it measures. Which changes should the pipeline adopt?
options: Require every finding to carry its source's publication date and the period the figure measures as structured fields.
Have doc-analysis keep the figure from the more recently published source and record the discarded value in a footnote.
Have synthesis average the two values and report the mean, citing both sources so the spread stays visible to readers.
Add a verify_fact call on each numeric claim and keep whichever value verification reports as the one currently in use.
Have synthesis compare those periods before it flags a conflict, so figures covering the same period are still escalated.
cards.a: A. Require every finding to carry its source's publication date and the period the figure measures as structured fields.; E. Have synthesis compare those periods before it flags a conflict, so figures covering the same period are still escalated.
cards.explanation:
A. Correct. Dates in the structured output are what let a reader or a downstream agent see that an annual total and a quarterly total are not in conflict at all, and they cost one field per finding.

B. Preferring the newer publication resolves the pair quickly and keeps a trace of the loser, but publication date is not measurement period, and a 2025 quarterly figure would silently displace a sound annual one.

C. Averaging yields one tidy number with both citations attached, yet it publishes a figure neither source stands behind and blends two quantities that were never measuring the same span of time.

D. Verification confirms that a claim really appears in its cited source and would catch a misread number, but it cannot judge which of two accurate figures from different periods belongs in the report.

E. Correct. Dates only help if something reads them: comparing measurement periods first lets a timing difference be explained rather than escalated, while a genuine same-period disagreement still reaches the coordinator.

Key principle: Numbers that disagree are not automatically contradictory. Carry publication and collection dates through the structured output and compare them before judging, so timing differences and real disagreements are told apart.

cards.q: Extraction accuracy measures 97% overall and the AP director wants human review dropped for high-confidence results. Shipping manifests are about a fifth of volume and were the most recent document type added to the pipeline. What must you establish before reducing review?
options: Raise the confidence threshold for routing to review, so only the safest extractions skip a reviewer.
Break the accuracy measurement out by document type and by field, and confirm every segment holds.
Sample the lowest-confidence extractions weekly and measure how often a reviewer changes the value.
Track the ledger's downstream correction rate for a month and cut review if the rate stays flat.
cards.a: B. Break the accuracy measurement out by document type and by field, and confirm every segment holds.
cards.explanation:
A. A higher threshold is a sensible lever once you know what confidence is worth, and it does shrink the automated population. Applied to an unvalidated aggregate it just moves an unknown line: if manifests are the weak segment, a stricter global threshold still automates whichever manifest extractions happen to score high.

B. Correct. A 97% aggregate can conceal a much worse rate on a segment that is only a fifth of volume, and the newest document type is the likeliest place for it to hide. Accuracy has to hold per document type and per field before any of it is automated away.

C. Sampling low-confidence extractions tells you whether the review queue is worth its cost, which is a fair question. It measures the population you are keeping under review rather than the population you are about to stop reviewing - the high-confidence results are where the risk of this change sits.

D. Watching downstream corrections is a real production signal and worth instrumenting either way. It is also lagging and lossy: ledger errors surface late, only some are traced back, and a flat rate during a month of full human review says nothing about what happens once review is removed.

Key principle: Aggregate accuracy can mask poor performance on a specific document type or field. Validate accuracy by segment - and especially on recently added types - before automating high-confidence extractions.

cards.q: Per-document extractions pass through a per-vendor compaction step before a synthesis agent rolls them into the monthly spend report. An AP clerk questions one line and nobody can say which invoice or manifest produced the figure: compaction kept the numbers and discarded the rest. Which two changes restore traceability?
options: Require each extraction to emit a mapping from every field it returns to the document and page behind it.
Have the synthesis agent reopen the underlying documents to locate the origin of any figure a clerk queries.
Define the compaction output schema so that a retained figure carries its source reference through to synthesis.
Send the full uncompacted extractions straight to synthesis so that nothing about a figure is dropped before the roll-up.
Have the report state that a line may aggregate several documents and link readers to that month's archive.
cards.a: A. Require each extraction to emit a mapping from every field it returns to the document and page behind it.; C. Define the compaction output schema so that a retained figure carries its source reference through to synthesis.
cards.explanation:
A. Correct. Attribution has to exist as structured data before anything downstream can preserve it. A field-to-document mapping produced at extraction time is the record that later steps carry forward.

B. Reopening documents does answer the occasional one-off question and needs no pipeline change. It reconstructs attribution by searching for a matching number after the fact, which is guesswork once several vendors report similar totals in one month.

C. Correct. Compression is where attribution is lost, so the compaction schema is what has to guarantee it survives. Requiring each retained figure to keep its source reference makes the mapping traverse the summarisation step intact.

D. Skipping compaction does keep every detail available and would work for a small month. A month of nightly runs will not fit one synthesis step, and raw extraction text still leaves the agent inferring which document a figure came from rather than reading it.

E. A caveat on the report is honest about the aggregation and costs nothing to add. It tells the clerk that the answer is unavailable rather than supplying it, and an archive link without a per-figure reference leaves the same manual search.

Key principle: Source attribution is lost at summarisation steps unless claim-to-source mappings are produced upstream and required to survive every compression between extraction and synthesis.
